chapters.title: Number operations, factors and remainders

concepts.title: Factor before calculating
concepts.text: Prime factorisation expresses a positive integer as prime powers. The HCF takes common primes to their smaller powers; the LCM takes all primes to their larger powers. For two positive integers, HCF × LCM equals their product.

concepts.title: Keep operations explicit
concepts.text: Evaluate brackets, then powers, then multiplication/division from left to right, then addition/subtraction. Division is not commutative. A remainder on division by a positive d must lie from 0 to d−1.

concepts.title: Convert rather than guess
concepts.text: A terminating decimal can be written over a power of ten and reduced. A square root is the nonnegative root by convention: √49=7, while solving x²=49 gives x=±7.

example.problem: Find HCF and LCM of 72 and 120, and simplify 3/4 + 0.125.

chapters.mistake: A square-root expression and the solutions to a squared equation are different.

chapters.title: Algebra, surds and linear graphs

concepts.title: Use identities with conditions
concepts.text: (a+b)²=a²+2 ab+b² and a²−b²=(a−b)(a+b). For x≠0, (x+1/x)²=x²+2+1/x². State nonzero denominators before rearranging.

concepts.title: Isolate and check
concepts.text: Apply the same operation to both sides of an equation. Substitute the proposed solution into the original equation. For y=mx+c, m is slope and c the y-intercept.

concepts.title: Simplify radicals
concepts.text: For nonnegative a,b, √(ab)=√a√b. Factor out perfect squares. In general √(a+b) is not √a+√b.

example.problem: If x+1/x=5, find x²+1/x². Also simplify √72.
steps: Square the equation:25=x²+2+1/x².
Subtract 2 to obtain 23.

chapters.mistake: Do not drop the middle term 2 ab in a squared sum.

chapters.title: Mixtures, alligation and partnership

concepts.title: Conserve the measured amount
concepts.text: For mixtures, total solute equals concentration×volume when the stated units and additive-volume assumption apply. The weighted concentration lies between component concentrations.

concepts.title: Use alligation only with a valid average
concepts.text: For low concentration L, high H and desired M with L<M<H, low:high=(H−M):(M−L). The ratio refers to quantities, not prices unless it is a price-mixture problem.

concepts.title: Weight partnership by time
concepts.text: When profit is shared in proportion to invested capital over time, use capital×duration. This is a stated model; real agreements can specify a different rule.

example.problem: Mix 20% and 50% solutions to obtain 30 litres at 30%. Separately compare ₹4,000 invested for 12 months and ₹6,000 for 8 months.
steps: Volumes 20 L and 10 L; solute=4+5=9 L, which is 30% of 30 L.
Capital-time products are both 48,000 rupee-months.

chapters.mistake: Averaging concentrations without their quantities gives the wrong mixture.
recall: Use alligation only with a valid average

chapters.title: Triangles, centres and similarity

concepts.title: Angles and length constraints
concepts.text: Triangle angles sum to 180°. The sum of any two side lengths must exceed the third. In a right triangle, hypotenuse² equals the sum of the squares of the legs.

concepts.title: Distinguish congruence and similarity
concepts.text: Congruent triangles have equal corresponding sides and angles. Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional sides. If length scale is k, area scale is k².

concepts.title: Know each centre by construction
concepts.text: Medians meet at the centroid, which divides each median 2:1 from the vertex. Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre; angle bisectors at the incentre; altitudes at the orthocentre.

example.problem: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12 cm. A similar triangle has corresponding lengths doubled. Find each hypotenuse and the area ratio.
steps: Hypotenuse=√(81+144)=15 cm.
Length scale 2 gives the other hypotenuse 30 cm.
Area scale=2²=4.

chapters.mistake: Doubling side length quadruples area, rather than doubling it.

chapters.title: Circles, chords and tangents

concepts.title: Use the radius at contact
concepts.text: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its contact point. Tangent segments from the same external point to a circle have equal lengths.

concepts.title: Relate angles to an arc
concepts.text: The angle at the centre is twice an angle at the circumference subtending the same arc under the usual configuration. An angle in a semicircle is 90°. Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.

concepts.title: Draw the hidden right triangle
concepts.text: For an external point at distance d from a centre of radius r, tangent length is √(d²−r²), with d>r. A perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it.

example.problem: A point lies 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find a tangent length.
steps: Join centre, contact point and external point.
The radius and tangent meet at 90°.
Tangent²=13²−5²=144.

chapters.mistake: A line through the centre is not generally a tangent.

chapters.title: Plane areas and solid volumes

concepts.title: Separate length, area and volume
concepts.text: A rectangle has area lb; a triangle½bh; a circleπr². Scaling all lengths by k scales surface area by k² and volume by k³. Convert units before substituting.

concepts.title: Use base area and perpendicular height
concepts.text: Prism volume is base area×height. A pyramid or cone has one third of that corresponding volume. For a cylinder V=πr²h; sphere V=4πr³/3; hemisphere V=2πr³/3.

concepts.title: Specify which surface
concepts.text: Cylinder curved area=2πrh and total area=2πr(h+r). A hemisphere has curved area 2πr² and total area 3πr². Cone slant height differs from perpendicular height.

example.problem: A cylinder has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Usingπ=22/7 find volume and curved surface area.
steps: Curved area=2×(22/7)×7×10=440 cm².
The two circular bases add 308 cm² if total area is needed.

chapters.mistake: Do not add a surface area to a volume.
recall: Use base area and perpendicular height

chapters.title: Trigonometric ratios, identities and heights

concepts.title: Label sides relative to the angle
concepts.text: In a right triangle, sinθ=opposite/hypotenuse, cosθ=adjacent/hypotenuse and tanθ=opposite/adjacent. The opposite side changes when the reference acute angle changes.

concepts.title: Use identities without inventing values
concepts.text: sin²θ+cos²θ=1 and tanθ=sinθ/cosθ when cosθ≠0. For acute θ, sin(90°−θ)=cosθ. π radians=180°. Standard values should be derived from familiar right triangles.

concepts.title: Model the height problem
concepts.text: An angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal. For a level ground baseline d and angle θ, height difference=d tanθ. Add observer eye height only if it is supplied.

example.problem: A tower is observed from level ground 30 m away at 45°. The observer eye is 1.5 m above ground. Find tower height.
steps: Height above eye level=30 tan 45°=30 m.
Add the eye height 1.5 m.
Total height=31.5 m.

chapters.mistake: Do not add an invented eye height when a question gives none.
recall: Label sides relative to the angle

chapters.title: Tables, charts and percentage comparisons

concepts.title: Read the denominator and unit
concepts.text: Before calculating, record what each row and axis measures. A percentage of total uses the total, while growth uses the earlier value. An average rate may need weighting.

concepts.title: Choose the right chart interpretation
concepts.text: Bar charts compare categories. A histogram describes intervals of numerical data; for unequal class widths, frequency density rather than raw height is relevant. A pie angle is 360°×category/total.

concepts.title: Check approximation
concepts.text: Estimate an answer to reject impossible options, then compute if choices are close. Distinguish a percentage change from a change in percentage points.

example.problem: A centre recorded 40,60,50 and 90 registrations in four weeks. Find the second week share and the pie angle for the fourth.
steps: Second week share=60/240=25%.
Fourth week angle=360×90/240=135°.

chapters.mistake: Changing shares and changing counts are not the same comparison.

chapters.title: Arithmetic applications and inverse percentages

concepts.title: Link the earlier foundation lessons
concepts.text: Use percentage multipliers for successive changes; use proportional parts for sharing; use work-per-time rather than completion times. These principles combine in multi-step SSC arithmetic problems.

concepts.title: Distinguish interest models
concepts.text: Simple interest=P×r×t. Compound amount=P(1+r/n)^(nt), with consistent annual rate and periods. A loan or bank product with fees is not described fully by these textbook models.

concepts.title: Reverse with algebra
concepts.text: If a value after a 20% increase is given, divide by 1.2. If work or distance remains, compute the remaining quantity before switching a rate.

example.problem: A quantity increases 20% to₹960, then a 10% discount is applied. Find its original and final values.

chapters.mistake: Successive percentage changes use different bases.

chapters.title: Series, analogies and classification

concepts.title: State a rule that fits every step
concepts.text: For a numerical series inspect differences, ratios and alternating subsequences. A finite sequence can admit multiple invented continuations; exam practice assumes the simplest intended rule among the options.

concepts.title: Preserve the relation
concepts.text: An analogy is a relation, not just two associated words. Identify part-to-whole, tool-to-purpose, opposite, category or a specified numerical operation, then apply the same relation.

concepts.title: Classify by one stated property
concepts.text: For an odd-one-out problem test a shared property. Explain why the chosen option differs; do not select based on superficial familiarity.

example.problem: Continue 3,8,15,24,35 using consecutive odd differences.
steps: Differences are 5,7,9,11.
Next difference is 13.

chapters.mistake: A plausible rule must explain every supplied term.
recall: State a rule that fits every step

chapters.title: Coding, alphabet positions and symbolic operations

concepts.title: Write the mapping explicitly
concepts.text: For a letter shift use A=1,…,Z=26 and define wraparound. Apply the same shift to each letter; test an example before transforming the target word.

concepts.title: Replace meanings before evaluating
concepts.text: If symbols represent different arithmetic operations, first rewrite the full expression using the defined meanings. Then follow normal order of operations unless the question supplies a different rule.

concepts.title: Check reversal and alternation
concepts.text: Some codes reverse order before shifting or use different rules at odd and even positions. A word pattern alone is not evidence that every letter follows one shift.

example.problem: If each letter is shifted forward 2 with wraparound, encode ZEBRA.
steps: Z wraps to B; E becomes G.
B→D, R→T, A→C.
Keep the original order of the transformed letters.

chapters.mistake: Do not forget wraparound afterZ.

chapters.title: Directions, distance and spatial orientation

concepts.title: Use coordinates
concepts.text: Choose east as positive x and north as positive y. Add each displacement separately. Straight-line distance uses the final net coordinates, not total path length.

concepts.title: Track heading separately from location
concepts.text: A left or right turn depends on the current heading. A half-turn reverses direction. For standard plan-view questions define the viewpoint instead of inferring a different one.

concepts.title: Distinguish path and displacement
concepts.text: Walking a closed route can have a positive path length but zero displacement. Pythagoras applies to perpendicular net components.

example.problem: Walk 8 m east,6 m north and 8 m west. Find final direction and distance from start.
steps: Net east displacement 8−8=0.
Net north displacement 6 m.
The final position is directly north of the start.

chapters.mistake: Path length and shortest distance answer different questions.

chapters.title: Family relations, ranks and ordered positions

concepts.title: Build only the stated relations
concepts.text: Record parent, child, sibling and spouse as distinct links. Do not infer gender from a name or assume every relative has only one sibling.

concepts.title: Turn ranks into positions
concepts.text: If the same person is kth from the left and rth from the right in a line, total=k+r−1. The middle person is counted twice before subtracting 1.

concepts.title: Handle inequalities consistently
concepts.text: For a>b and b>c, a>c follows. An equality can be substituted. A chain with missing comparisons may not fix the order of all participants.

example.problem: One student is 8th from the left and 12th from the right. How many students are in the line?
steps: Count 8 positions from the left including that student.
Count 12 from the right including the same student.
Subtract the duplicate count:8+12−1.

chapters.mistake: A relation can be possible without being forced by the information.

chapters.title: Venn diagrams, syllogisms and set counts

concepts.title: Represent all, some and none differently
concepts.text: All A are B means A is a subset of B; it does not imply all B are A. Some A are B asserts an overlap exists. No A are B means disjoint sets.

concepts.title: Avoid invented existence
concepts.text: In standard modern logical reading, an all-statement alone does not establish that A exists. A conclusion using some requires supplied existence. State the convention when solving a formal syllogism.

concepts.title: Subtract overlap once
concepts.text: For two sets, |A∪B|=|A|+|B|−|A∩B|. Neither equals the universe size minus the union.

example.problem: Of 50 students,28 study French,24 study German and 10 study both. How many study neither?
steps: Subtract union from total 50.
Neither=8.

chapters.mistake: Do not count the overlap twice.
recall: Represent all, some and none differently

chapters.title: Seating, scheduling and constraint tables

concepts.title: Fix a coordinate convention
concepts.text: Number positions from the reader’s left. For circular seating, specify whether people face inward or outward before interpreting left and right. Identify immediate adjacency separately from a general left-of relation.

concepts.title: Use a constraint table
concepts.text: Mark fixed positions, exclusions and relative blocks. Carry each condition into every candidate. Do not complete a diagram with an unstated assumption.

concepts.title: Check every candidate
concepts.text: A unique answer follows only if all valid arrangements agree on the requested fact. If two satisfy the conditions with different answers, report insufficient information instead of choosing one.

example.problem: Three talks X,Y,Z occur on Monday,Tuesday,Wednesday. X is before Y and Z is not on Wednesday. Find all schedules.
steps: X before Y givesXY as an ordered pair.
List XYZ,XZY,ZXY.
XYZ has Z on Wednesday and is rejected; XZY and ZXY remain.
example.answer: Two schedules remain; Y is on Wednesday in both.

chapters.mistake: One working diagram does not prove uniqueness.

chapters.title: Non-verbal reasoning: transformations and patterns

concepts.title: Describe the transformation
concepts.text: Reflection across a vertical mirror reverses left and right; a horizontal water-line reflection reverses up and down. Rotation preserves handedness; reflection reverses it. Name the mirror axis.

concepts.title: Track labelled parts
concepts.text: Use arrows, corners and labelled points rather than guessing from overall resemblance. In paper-folding questions, reflect holes across each fold in reverse order; holes on a fold can coincide.

concepts.title: Respect what a text sketch cannot show
concepts.text: Real embedded-figure and folded-paper practice needs legible diagrams. Use the linked official/free study resources for visual exercises; text-described transformations below train only the specified operations.

example.problem: An arrow points east. Reflect it in a vertical mirror, then rotate the result 90° clockwise.
steps: Vertical reflection turns east to west.
A clockwise quarter-turn from west points north.
Keep the order:reflection followed by rotation.

chapters.mistake: Reflecting and rotating in the opposite order can change the result.
recall: Respect what a text sketch cannot show

chapters.title: Critical reasoning and social judgement

concepts.title: Separate evidence and inference
concepts.text: A claim is what is asserted; evidence supports it; an assumption connects them. A correlation does not by itself identify a cause. Words like all and never require stronger evidence than some.

concepts.title: Use proportional responses
concepts.text: In workplace scenarios, identify the immediate risk, verify facts, communicate respectfully and use the relevant procedure. Emotional intelligence concerns recognising and regulating emotions, not suppressing every disagreement.

concepts.title: Compare exact information
concepts.text: For code or address matching, compare each required character and field. Avoid treating a visually similar letter and numeral as identical unless the question says they are.

example.problem: Visits rose after a library extended hours and a bus route opened. Is it established that extended hours alone caused the rise?
steps: Two changes occurred together.
The report does not isolate either effect.
A comparison or other causal design would be needed.
example.answer: No; the stated observations do not isolate the cause.

chapters.mistake: Do not replace an association with a causal certainty.

chapters.title: Grammar: subjects, agreement and sentence structure

concepts.title: Find the head of the subject
concepts.text: A phrase between subject and verb does not normally change the head noun’s number. In standard formal English, each and every take a singular verb when they head the subject.

concepts.title: Distinguish clause roles
concepts.text: A complete independent clause normally has a subject and a finite verb. A dependent clause introduced by although or because needs a main clause to complete its role in a sentence.

concepts.title: Edit for the intended meaning
concepts.text: Collective nouns and proximity constructions can vary by dialect and meaning. Use unambiguous standard examples for these drills; do not generalise a shortcut to every collective noun.

example.problem: Correct: Each of the files have a label.
steps: Head of the subject is Each, not files.
Each takes singular has in this construction.
Keep the rest of the sentence.
example.answer: Each of the files has a label.

chapters.mistake: Matching the verb to the nearest noun can hide the real subject.
recall: Find the head of the subject

chapters.title: Tense, aspect and conditional meaning

concepts.title: Locate the event in time
concepts.text: Simple past describes a completed past event; present perfect connects a past event to the present without a finished past-time marker in standard usage. The choice depends on context, not only a memorised keyword.

concepts.title: Distinguish duration and completion
concepts.text: Continuous forms emphasise an ongoing activity; perfect forms locate an event before another reference point. State the reference time before choosing the verb.

concepts.title: Conditional structure carries meaning
concepts.text: For an ordinary real future condition, use if+present and will+base verb in the result. An unreal present hypothesis commonly uses if+past and would+base verb; formal were can mark a hypothetical condition.

example.problem: Choose the form for a completed action at a specified past time: She ___ the report yesterday.
steps: Yesterday is a finished past-time marker.
Use simple past for this event.
The irregular past of write is wrote.

chapters.mistake: Do not use present perfect mechanically with a finished-time marker like yesterday.

chapters.title: Articles, determiners and prepositions

concepts.title: Choose a/an by sound
concepts.text: Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound. Spelling alone is insufficient: a university begins with a consonant /y/ sound, while an hour begins with a vowel sound.

concepts.title: Use the when identification is specific
concepts.text: The points to an identified referent in context. Many general plural and uncountable nouns use no article. Article choice must be checked against the sentence meaning.

concepts.title: Learn prepositions in constructions
concepts.text: Interested in, good at and depend on are conventional patterns. Time expressions commonly use at for clock times, on for named days and in for months/years. Exceptions and idiomatic constructions require context.

example.problem: Fill the blanks: She is ___ honest person and studies at ___ university.
steps: Honest begins with a vowel sound because h is silent.
University begins with a consonant /y/ sound.
Choose an and a respectively.

chapters.mistake: Article selection follows pronunciation rather than the first written letter.
recall: Use the when identification is specific

chapters.title: Active and passive voice

concepts.title: Preserve tense and meaning
concepts.text: In a basic passive transformation, the active object becomes the passive subject; use the appropriate form of be plus the past participle. The agent can be introduced with by if relevant.

concepts.title: Check whether a passive is available
concepts.text: The basic object-to-subject transformation requires a transitive use. An intransitive clause such as She slept cannot be transformed by inventing an object.

concepts.title: Keep aspect and auxiliaries
concepts.text: Present continuous passive uses is/are being+participle; present perfect passive uses has/have been+participle. Do not drop a modal or change a negative into a positive.

example.problem: Transform: The clerk has checked the documents.
steps: Documents is the active object and becomes passive subject.
Plural subject uses have been checked.
The clerk may be retained as by the clerk.
example.answer: The documents have been checked by the clerk.

chapters.mistake: Changinghas checked towere checked loses the present-perfect meaning.
recall: Check whether a passive is available

chapters.title: Direct and reported speech

concepts.title: Report the message, not the quotation marks
concepts.text: Reported statements commonly use a reporting verb and a clause. Pronouns and place/time words must match who is reporting and when; they are not changed blindly.

concepts.title: Backshift with a past reporting context
concepts.text: In a conventional past reporting context, present simple often shifts to past simple and will to would. Backshift is not always required for a statement still true; the intended context decides.

concepts.title: Questions and commands differ
concepts.text: Reported questions use statement word order, with if/whether for yes–no questions. Commands commonly use told/asked+object+to-infinitive; a negative command uses not to.

example.problem: Report in a later past context: Mira said,"I am tired."
steps: Mira is the speaker, so I becomes she.
In this past reporting context am backshifts to was.
Remove quotation punctuation and form a reported statement.
example.answer: Mira said that she was tired.

chapters.mistake: Reported questions do not retain ordinary direct-question inversion.
recall: Report the message, not the quotation marks
Backshift with a past reporting context

chapters.title: Vocabulary, spelling and word formation

concepts.title: Choose meaning in context
concepts.text: Near-synonyms differ in register and sense. Confirm the meaning used in the sentence before replacing a word. An antonym must oppose that meaning, not an unrelated sense.

concepts.title: Distinguish sound and spelling
concepts.text: Homophones sound alike but can differ in spelling and meaning, such as principal and principle. A word-family suffix can change part of speech:careful is an adjective;carefully an adverb.

concepts.title: Use retrieval rather than passive rereading
concepts.text: Record a word, a concise meaning and your own sentence, then test recall later. A single list of words cannot represent complete vocabulary coverage.

example.problem: Choose principal or principle: Honesty is a guiding ___.
steps: The sentence refers to a rule or belief.
Principle names a rule or belief.
Principal can mean chief or a head of an institution.

chapters.mistake: Do not choose a homophone by sound alone.
recall: Use retrieval rather than passive rereading

chapters.title: Idioms, phrasal verbs and sentence improvement

concepts.title: Interpret a phrase as a unit
concepts.text: An idiom often has a conventional meaning not predictable from its separate words. In hit the nail on the head, the meaning is to identify something exactly, not necessarily to use a hammer.

concepts.title: Track particles and objects
concepts.text: Phrasal verbs such as put off can change meaning with context. An object pronoun can affect placement in separable constructions:put it off, not put off it in this meaning.

concepts.title: Improve only what is wrong
concepts.text: Preserve meaning and tense when editing. Avoid redundant combinations and unnatural collocations, but do not replace an acceptable sentence merely to make it longer.

example.problem: Improve: We discussed about the proposal.
steps: In this transitive use,discuss takes a direct object.
Remove about without changing the past tense.
Keep the original meaning.

chapters.mistake: A word-for-word translation from another language may introduce the wrong preposition.
recall: Interpret a phrase as a unit

chapters.title: Comprehension, cloze and paragraph order

concepts.title: Separate statement from inference
concepts.text: Summarise the passage’s central claim, identify the supporting sentence and reject an option that adds an unsupported absolute or cause. Answer from the supplied passage rather than outside assumptions.

concepts.title: Use cohesion for ordering
concepts.text: Pronouns need antecedents;therefore signals a consequence and however a contrast. A sentence introducing a new subject commonly precedes one referring back to this change.

concepts.title: Cloze decisions use grammar and meaning
concepts.text: Check part of speech, tense, agreement and collocation, then read the completed paragraph for coherence. A locally grammatical word can still contradict the passage.

example.problem: Original passage: A town added evening buses. Passenger trips rose, but the survey did not count distinct riders. Can we infer the number of distinct riders increased?
steps: The measured quantity is trips.
One rider may make several trips.
Distinct rider counts are not provided.
example.answer: No; only a rise in trips is established.

chapters.mistake: Do not treat more trips as proof of more people.
recall: Cloze decisions use grammar and meaning

chapters.title: Polity: institutions, rights and constitutional structure

concepts.title: Separate institutions and functions
concepts.text: Parliament legislates; the executive administers; courts adjudicate. India has a parliamentary system. Constitutional provisions distribute powers and provide checks; the categories are related rather than wholly isolated.

concepts.title: Distinguish rights and directives
concepts.text: Fundamental Rights are constitutionally protected with judicial remedies. Directive Principles guide state policy and are not directly enforceable by courts as rights. Neither a right nor a general policy slogan should be treated as unlimited.

concepts.title: Use dated primary text
concepts.text: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, with certain provisions effective earlier. For article numbers, amendments and exceptions consult the current official text; an old coaching chart is not the legal authority.

example.problem: A note calls every welfare goal in the Constitution directly enforceable. What distinction is missing?
steps: Identify whether the provision is a Fundamental Right or a Directive Principle.
Directive Principles guide policy but are non-justiciable.
The relevant provision and remedy must be checked individually.
example.answer: The note confuses constitutional policy guidance with directly enforceable rights.

chapters.mistake: Non-justiciable does not mean irrelevant to governance.

chapters.title: History: chronology, evidence and the national movement

concepts.title: Build a timeline before memorising isolated facts
concepts.text: Distinguish an event, its immediate objective and its wider context. Sequence is not proof that one event alone caused another. Political, social and economic processes can develop together.

concepts.title: Separate broad phases
concepts.text: For modern history, connect colonial expansion,1857, organised nationalism, mass movements and independence. For ancient and medieval history build parallel timelines of states, social change and cultural developments using the linked textbooks.

concepts.title: Assess historical evidence
concepts.text: A contemporary account is a primary source for what it records, but can reflect its author’s viewpoint. Compare sources and distinguish a later interpretation from an original record.

example.problem: Place the Revolt of 1857, the Salt March and Indian independence in chronological order.
steps: The revolt belongs to 1857.
The Salt March took place in 1930.
Independence followed in 1947.

chapters.mistake: Do not merge the dates of a movement, an act and an election.
recall: Build a timeline before memorising isolated facts

chapters.title: Geography: Earth, coordinates, climate and resources

concepts.title: Use coordinates correctly
concepts.text: Latitude measures angular position north or south of the equator; longitude measures east or west relative to a reference meridian. Coordinates are angles, not a direct distance in kilometres.

concepts.title: Distinguish rotation and revolution
concepts.text: Earth’s rotation produces the day–night cycle. Seasons arise mainly from axial tilt combined with Earth’s revolution around the Sun, not simply from changing Earth–Sun distance.

concepts.title: Link physical and human geography
concepts.text: Relief, drainage and climate influence settlement and resources, but do not determine every social outcome. Use maps to locate Indian rivers, mountain ranges, neighbouring countries and major resource regions rather than relying only on word lists.

example.problem: Explain why opposite hemispheres have different seasons at the same time.
steps: Earth’s axis is tilted relative to its orbit.
The hemispheres receive different sunlight angles and day lengths during the orbit.
When one is tilted toward the Sun, the other is tilted away.
example.answer: Opposite seasonal conditions follow from axial tilt and orbital position.

chapters.mistake: Day–night and seasonal change operate on different time scales.

chapters.title: Physics: units, motion, energy and everyday observations

concepts.title: Use quantities with units
concepts.text: Force is measured in newtons, energy/work in joules and power in watts. Speed is distance/time; acceleration is velocity change/time. Dimensions help identify an impossible formula.

concepts.title: Apply a model within its conditions
concepts.text: For constant acceleration,v=u+at. Work by a constant force parallel to displacement is Fs; power is work/time. Ohm’s law V=IR models an ohmic resistor under specified conditions.

concepts.title: Distinguish waves and transport
concepts.text: Sound is a mechanical wave requiring a medium. Light can propagate in vacuum. Refraction concerns a change of propagation direction associated with a change in wave speed at an interface, subject to incidence conditions.

example.problem: A machine performs 900 J of work in 30 s. Find its average power.
steps: Power=work/time.
J/s is the watt.

chapters.mistake: Energy and power are different physical quantities.
recall: Apply a model within its conditions

chapters.title: Chemistry: atoms, reactions, acids and materials

concepts.title: Keep atomic quantities distinct
concepts.text: Atomic number counts protons. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons. Isotopes of an element have the same proton count but different neutron counts.

concepts.title: Separate physical and chemical changes
concepts.text: A physical change can alter state without changing chemical identity. A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into different substances. Balance equations by conserving each element’s atom count, not by altering chemical formula subscripts.

concepts.title: Interpret acidity within conditions
concepts.text: In the usual dilute aqueous school model at 25°C,pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 basic; neutral water has pH 7. Acids and bases can neutralise, but products and hazards depend on the substances and conditions.

example.problem: Balance hydrogen reacting with oxygen to form water.
steps: Start H₂+O₂→H₂O.
Put 2 before H₂O to balance oxygen.
Put 2 before H₂ to balance hydrogen.

chapters.mistake: Change coefficients to balance atoms; changing a subscript changes the substance.

chapters.title: Biology: cells, life processes and ecology

concepts.title: Start from cell organisation
concepts.text: Cells are basic units of life. Eukaryotic cells contain a membrane-bound nucleus; prokaryotic cells lack one. A virus is not a cellular organism and depends on a host’s machinery for replication.

concepts.title: Distinguish key processes
concepts.text: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical forms in photosynthetic organisms. Cellular respiration transfers energy from fuel molecules into usable cellular energy. Plants carry out respiration as well as photosynthesis.

concepts.title: Connect organisms to environments
concepts.text: Producers, consumers and decomposers have different ecological roles. Energy flows through food chains while matter cycles. Health topics here are general science revision, not diagnosis or treatment instructions.

example.problem: A statement says plants photosynthesise and therefore never respire. Is it correct?
steps: Photosynthesis and respiration are distinct processes.
Plant cells require usable energy.
Plants also carry out cellular respiration.
example.answer: No; photosynthesis does not exclude respiration.

chapters.mistake: Do not treat a broad contrast as an absolute exceptionless rule.

chapters.title: Economy, culture and current-affairs source literacy

concepts.title: Separate stocks and flows
concepts.text: A stock is measured at a point in time; a flow over a period. GDP is a production flow over a stated period. A price-level index and its rate of change are different quantities.

concepts.title: Identify policy instruments
concepts.text: Fiscal policy concerns government taxation and spending. Monetary policy concerns monetary conditions and related central-bank tools. Public policy announcements are not by themselves evidence that the stated outcome has occurred.

concepts.title: Build dated culture and news records
concepts.text: For culture, organise traditions by region, period and evidence. For news, store the original issuer, event date, publication date and subsequent corrections. No five-year topic-frequency or high-weightage claim is made without an auditable paper dataset.

example.problem: A report says an index rose from 120 to 126 in one year. Find percentage growth and explain what the index level alone cannot establish.
steps: The level 126 is not itself a 126% annual growth rate.
Interpretation also requires the index definition and base.
example.answer: 5% growth; the index level alone is not the growth rate.

chapters.mistake: Do not confuse a policy target with measured achievement.
recall: Build dated culture and news records

chapters.title: Computer hardware, memory and operating systems

concepts.title: Follow the data path
concepts.text: Input devices capture data; the CPU executes instructions using registers and memory; output devices present results. A touchscreen can serve both input and output roles. A port is an interface, not itself a storage capacity.

concepts.title: Separate volatile and persistent storage
concepts.text: RAM normally loses its contents without power. SSDs and hard drives retain files. Capacity and access speed describe different properties. A byte is eight bits; binary KiB is 1024 bytes, while decimal kB is 1000 bytes.

concepts.title: Use the operating system
concepts.text: An operating system manages processes, memory, devices and files. Windows File Explorer organises files and folders; an extension suggests a format but renaming it does not convert the contents. Deleting to a recycle bin and permanently deleting are different operations.

example.problem: A file contains 4096 bytes. Express its size in KiB, and identify where an unsaved document may be lost during power failure.
steps: Use 1 KiB=1024 bytes.
Unsaved work held only in volatile memory can be lost.
example.answer: 4 KiB; volatile memory does not guarantee persistence.

chapters.mistake: Do not treat RAM capacity as the same as SSD capacity.

chapters.title: Word processing, presentations and file workflows

concepts.title: Choose the right document tool
concepts.text: A word processor manages text, styles, tables and page layout. A presentation arranges content into slides. Styles provide consistent heading structure; manually making every heading large does not create the same structural information.

concepts.title: Distinguish operations
concepts.text: Copy duplicates selected content; cut removes it for a move; paste inserts clipboard content. Save updates the working file; Save As can create another file or format. In common Windows desktop applications Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V and Ctrl+Z mean copy, cut, paste and undo, but shortcuts can vary by application.

concepts.title: Keep outputs usable
concepts.text: Page orientation changes the page layout, not the meaning of the text. A slide transition acts between slides, while an animation acts on an object. Preview printing and export before sharing; inspect the actual exported file rather than trusting its extension.

example.problem: A report needs consistent chapter headings and a second copy under a new name. Which operations fit?
steps: Apply a heading style to chapter titles.
Use Save As to create a separately named copy.
Open the copy to check content and layout.

chapters.mistake: A slide animation is not a transition between slides.

chapters.title: Excel formulas, references and functions

concepts.title: Start a formula explicitly
concepts.text: In Excel a formula begins with =. A1 names a cell by column and row. A1:A4 is an inclusive range. SUM adds numerical values; AVERAGE returns their arithmetic mean, while COUNT counts numeric entries rather than every nonempty cell.

concepts.title: Track reference movement
concepts.text: Relative A1 shifts when copied. Absolute $A$1 fixes both coordinates. Mixed $A1 fixes the column and A$1 fixes the row. Predict the copied formula before calculating its value.

concepts.title: Separate storage from display
concepts.text: A displayed percentage is a format for an underlying value. A cell containing 0.25 can display 25%. Formatting a cell does not necessarily change its stored number. Parentheses control arithmetic grouping in formulas.

example.problem: B2 contains =A2*$D$1. What is the formula after copying it to B3?
steps: B2 to B3 moves down one row.
Relative A2 becomes A3.
Absolute $D$1 stays fixed.

chapters.mistake: Do not freeze a row when the dollar sign fixes only a column.

chapters.title: Networks, email and safe digital transactions

concepts.title: Name the network role
concepts.text: A browser requests and displays web resources. A search engine indexes and retrieves information. A URL identifies a resource; DNS maps domain names to network information. Upload sends data from the local device to a remote service; download brings it back.

concepts.title: Use email fields deliberately
concepts.text: To identifies main recipients; CC copies visible recipients; BCC conceals that recipient list from other recipients. Reply All includes the relevant original recipients and should be inspected before sending. An attachment can carry malware even when its filename looks familiar.

concepts.title: Check identity before action
concepts.text: Phishing impersonates a trusted party to obtain credentials or payments. HTTPS protects a connection but does not prove the operator is honest. Use updates, backups, unique passwords and multi-factor authentication. Never share an OTP or approve an unsolicited payment request to receive money.

example.problem: An unsolicited message asks for your bank OTP and links to a similar-looking domain. What is the appropriate response?
steps: Do not enter the OTP or use the message link.
Open the bank through an independently known official channel.
Report the suspicious message using that channel.
example.answer: Verify independently; do not share the OTP.

chapters.mistake: A padlock is not a guarantee that a website is trustworthy.

chapters.title: Statistics: data, centre, dispersion and moments

concepts.title: Identify the observational unit
concepts.text: Separate a population from a sample and a variable from its observed values. Categories, discrete counts and continuous measurements require appropriate tables and plots. A frequency table must account for every observation exactly once.

concepts.title: Choose centre and spread together
concepts.text: Mean=sum/n; median is the middle ordered value, averaging the two middle values for even n. The mode is the most frequent value and need not be unique. Range=max−min. Population variance averages squared deviations using n; the usual unbiased sample variance uses n−1.

concepts.title: Describe shape carefully
concepts.text: Central moments use deviations from the mean. Standardised third and fourth moments describe skewness and kurtosis; conventions for excess kurtosis subtract 3. Quartiles depend on a stated finite-sample convention. A coefficient of variation requires a meaningful nonzero mean and ratio-scale interpretation.

example.problem: For the full population {2,4,6}, find mean and population variance.
steps: Squared deviations are 4,0,4.
Population variance=8/3; sample variance for these observations would be 4.

chapters.mistake: Do not switch n and n−1 without naming the target.

chapters.title: Statistics: probability and random variables

concepts.title: Condition on the given event
concepts.text: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0. Independence means P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), whereas disjoint positive-probability events cannot be independent. Bayes theorem reverses conditioning using prior probabilities and likelihoods.

concepts.title: Calculate expectation from a distribution
concepts.text: For discrete X, E[X]=Σxp(x) and Var(X)=E[X²]−E[X]². A valid probability mass function is nonnegative and sums to one. Joint distributions yield marginals by summing over the other variable; independence requires factorisation.

concepts.title: Match a model to assumptions
concepts.text: Binomial counts successes in n independent equal-p trials, mean np and variance np(1−p). Poisson has mean and variance λ. A normal distribution uses mean μ and variance σ². Exponential waiting time with rate λ has mean 1/λ. Model assumptions must be justified, not chosen just from a formula.

example.problem: X has probabilities P(X=0)=1/4 and P(X=2)=3/4. Find its mean and variance.
steps: Variance=3−1.5²=0.75.

chapters.mistake: Mutually exclusive and independent are different conditions.

chapters.title: Statistics: sampling, estimation and tests

concepts.title: Define a sampling design
concepts.text: Simple random sampling gives each eligible sample of the stated size equal selection probability. Stratification samples within defined strata; clusters sample groups. Systematic sampling uses a start and interval, with periodicity risk. Convenience and purposive samples are not probability designs. Sampling and nonsampling errors require different controls.

concepts.title: Distinguish estimator properties
concepts.text: An estimator is a statistic used for an unknown parameter. Unbiasedness concerns its expectation; consistency concerns convergence with sample size. Method of moments matches sample and model moments; maximum likelihood maximises the likelihood over permitted parameter values. A confidence interval describes a procedure, not a posterior probability unless a Bayesian model is specified.

concepts.title: State assumptions before testing
concepts.text: A p-value is computed under the null model and is not the probability that the null is true. Type I error rejects a true null; power is 1−Type II error. Choice among z, t, chi-square and F procedures depends on model, sample and target. ANOVA compares mean variation between groups with residual variation under its assumptions; one-way and two-way designs use different decompositions.

example.problem: For independent normal observations with unknown variance, n=16, mean=12 and s=4, express the usual two-sided 95% mean interval.
steps: Use Student t with 15 degrees of freedom.
Standard error=s/√n=1.
Interval is 12±t(0.975,15)×1, approximately 12±2.131.

chapters.mistake: A small p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect.

chapters.title: Statistics: association, time series and index numbers

concepts.title: Separate association and prediction
concepts.text: Pearson correlation measures linear association and lies between −1 and 1 when defined. Spearman uses ranks. In simple least-squares regression with an intercept, slope b=r(sy/sx). Correlation is symmetric; regression of Y on X and X on Y solves different prediction problems. Partial correlation controls specified additional variables and does not by itself establish causality.

concepts.title: Decompose temporal change
concepts.text: Trend is long-run movement; seasonality repeats at a fixed within-year period. Moving averages can smooth fluctuations but do not prove an underlying causal mechanism. Additive models express components as a sum; multiplicative models use products and require suitable nonzero scaling.

concepts.title: Keep index weights explicit
concepts.text: A price relative is current/base×100. Laspeyres price index uses base-period quantities; Paasche uses current quantities. Base shifting rescales a consistently defined index. Splicing joins compatible series using an overlap, while changed coverage requires more than arithmetic. Cost-of-living indices concern a specified consumption basket or framework.

example.problem: Given r=0.6, sx=2 and sy=5, find the regression slope for predicting Y from X.
steps: Use b=r sy/sx.
Substitute 0.6×5/2.
Obtain 1.5; an intercept still needs the means.

chapters.mistake: A high correlation does not isolate the cause of an observed change.

chapters.title: Accounts: principles, journals, ledgers and reconciliation

concepts.title: Use the accounting equation
concepts.text: Assets=Liabilities+Equity. Double entry records equal debits and credits. Under conventional account rules, asset increases are debits and liability/equity increases are credits; expenses usually debit and revenue usually credits. Accrual recording follows earned revenue and incurred expense, not only cash movement.

concepts.title: Trace a transaction
concepts.text: Source documents support journal entries, which post to ledger accounts and feed a trial balance. Agreement of debit and credit totals does not detect every error: complete omission or an equal wrong-account posting can still balance. Rectification must follow the actual error rather than force a total.

concepts.title: Reconcile timing differences
concepts.text: Bank reconciliation explains differences between the cash-book bank balance and bank statement. A cheque issued but not presented and a deposit not yet credited are timing items. Bank charges not yet recorded require cash-book adjustment. Specify overdraft signs before adding or subtracting.

example.problem: A business buys equipment for cash ₹20,000. Explain the double entry and net effect on total assets.
steps: Debit equipment ₹20,000.
Credit cash ₹20,000.
One asset increases while another decreases equally.

chapters.mistake: A balanced trial balance is not proof that all records are correct.

chapters.title: Accounts: statements, depreciation, inventory and special records

concepts.title: Separate period performance and position
concepts.text: A trading account derives gross profit from net sales and cost of goods sold; further expenses and income determine net profit. A balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and equity at a date. Capital expenditure creates or improves a qualifying longer-term resource; revenue expenditure relates to current operations. Classification depends on substance.

concepts.title: Allocate costs systematically
concepts.text: Straight-line annual depreciation=(cost−residual value)/useful life under stable assumptions. Diminishing-balance depreciation applies a rate to carrying amount. Cost of goods sold=opening inventory+purchases−closing inventory in a simple periodic model. Inventory valuation rules and write-downs require the applicable accounting framework.

concepts.title: Recognise specialised records
concepts.text: A not-for-profit receipts-and-payments account tracks cash; an income-and-expenditure account uses accrual adjustments. A bill of exchange is a written payment order subject to its legal requirements; distinguish drawer, drawee and payee. Self-balancing ledgers use control/adjustment accounts to allow separate ledger balancing, not to remove double entry.

example.problem: Equipment costs ₹50,000, residual value ₹5,000 and useful life 5 years. Find straight-line annual depreciation and carrying amount after 2 full years.
steps: Depreciable amount=50,000−5,000=45,000.
Annual charge=45,000/5=9,000.

chapters.mistake: Receipts are not automatically revenue for the current period.

chapters.title: Economics: demand, production, cost and markets

concepts.title: Read the condition ceteris paribus
concepts.text: A demand curve relates own price and quantity demanded holding other determinants constant; income or preferences can shift it. Own-price elasticity=(percentage change in quantity)/(percentage change in price), with sign and measurement convention stated. Income and cross-price elasticities answer different questions.

concepts.title: Connect consumer and producer choices
concepts.text: Marshallian marginal utility and indifference-curve analysis are distinct consumer frameworks. A production possibility curve represents feasible output combinations under stated resources and technology. Short-run diminishing marginal product is not the same as long-run returns to scale, where all inputs vary.

concepts.title: Use marginal comparisons
concepts.text: Average cost=total cost/output; marginal cost is the additional cost of extra output. Under ideal price-taking conditions marginal revenue equals market price. Monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly differ in barriers, differentiation and strategic interaction. A competitive benchmark requires its assumptions, not merely many visible shops.

example.problem: Using initial-value percentages, price rises from 10 to 11 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. Find own-price elasticity.
steps: Price change=1/10=10%.
Quantity change=−20/100=−20%.
Elasticity=−20/10=−2. A midpoint method would produce a different numerical estimate.

chapters.mistake: A movement along demand is not the same as a demand shift.

chapters.title: Economics and governance: income, public finance and institutions

concepts.title: Measure the economy consistently
concepts.text: GDP counts final production within a territory over a period. Nominal measures use current prices; real measures adjust for price changes. Value added avoids double counting intermediate output. Poverty, unemployment and population indicators require a defined denominator, reference period and measurement method. Sector shares and infrastructure claims must be dated.

concepts.title: Distinguish policy and external accounts
concepts.text: Fiscal policy uses government revenue and expenditure; monetary policy addresses monetary conditions through the central bank and its framework. A fiscal deficit is not the same as public debt. The balance of payments records resident/nonresident economic transactions under an accounting framework. The 1991 reform discussion includes liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation; individual outcomes need evidence.

concepts.title: Know institutional mandates
concepts.text: The CAG audits public accounts within its constitutional and legal remit. The Finance Commission recommends specified fiscal arrangements, including tax distribution, under Article 280. RBI, commercial banks, regional rural banks and payments banks have different roles. FRBM refers to the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management framework; use current official texts for amendments and targets. IT governance includes accountable digital service delivery, access and data security, not simply installing computers.

example.problem: A firm buys intermediate inputs worth 70 and sells final output for 120. Find its value added, ignoring inventory changes.
steps: Count output at 120.
Subtract intermediate consumption 70.
Value added=50, avoiding repeated counting of the inputs.

chapters.mistake: Do not use an undated policy target as a current measured outcome.

questions.stem: What is the LCM of 18 and 24?
Simplify 3/5 + 0.25.
What is the remainder when 347 is divided by 9?
Evaluate 36÷6×3−4.
questions.explanation: Division and multiplication left to right:6×3−4=14.

questions.stem: If x+1/x=4, what is x²+1/x²?
questions.explanation: Square 4 and subtract 2:16−2=14.

questions.stem: Solve 3 x−7=20.
Simplify √50+√8.
What is the slope of y=−3 x+5?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of x in slope-intercept form is−3.

questions.stem: 10 L at 20% is mixed with 30 L at 40%. What is the concentration?
questions.explanation: Solute=2+12=14 L in 40 L, hence 35%.

questions.stem: Mix 10% and 40% solutions to get 20%. What is low:high?
A invests₹3,000 for 12 months and B₹6,000 for 6 months. Under capital-time sharing, what is A:B?
questions.explanation: Both products equal 36,000.

questions.stem: A mixture is 25% salt by mass. How much salt is in 12 kg of it?
A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. What is its hypotenuse?
Two angles of a triangle are 48° and 67°. Find the third.
The medians of a triangle meet at the:
questions.explanation: The centroid is the intersection of the three medians.

questions.stem: Similar triangles have side ratio 3:5. What is their area ratio?
questions.explanation: Square the side ratio:9:25.

questions.stem: An external point is 10 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm. Find the tangent length.
An angle subtended by a diameter at a point on the circle is:
questions.explanation: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

questions.stem: One angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is 112°. Its opposite angle is:
questions.explanation: Opposite angles sum to 180°, so 68°.

questions.stem: Two tangent segments from one external point are 7 cm and x cm. Find x.
questions.explanation: Tangent segments from the same external point are equal.

questions.stem: A cone has radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm. With π=22/7, find volume.
A square side increases from 4 to 6. Its area increases by:
If a sphere radius doubles, its volume becomes:
questions.explanation: Volume scales as the cube of radius.

questions.stem: Find the area of a triangle with base 14 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm.
questions.explanation: Area=½×14×9=63 cm².

questions.stem: If sinθ=3/5 for an acute angle, what is cosθ?
questions.explanation: cosθ=√(1−9/25)=4/5; acute makes it positive.

questions.stem: Evaluate sin²37°+cos²37°.
questions.explanation: The Pythagorean identity gives 1.

questions.stem: Convert π/3 radians to degrees.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 180/π to obtain 60°.

questions.stem: A tower is 20 m away on level ground and its elevation is 45° from a ground-level point. Find height.
A table has values 30,50,70 and 50. What share is the value 70?
A category represents 15% of a pie chart. What is its angle?
A rate rises from 20% to 25%. What is the increase in percentage points?
questions.explanation: 25−20=5 percentage points; relative increase is 25%.

questions.stem: For unequal-width histogram classes, frequency is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Frequency density×class width gives frequency, so bar area matters.

questions.stem: A value rises 25% to₹1,000. What was its original value?
A and B share₹3,600 in 2:7. What is B’s share?
questions.explanation: One part 400; B receives 7×400=2800.

questions.stem: A person covers 120 km at 40 km/h and 120 km at 60 km/h. Find average speed.
questions.explanation: Time=3+2=5 h, distance 240 km; average 48 km/h.

questions.stem: Simple interest on₹2,400 at 5% annually for 18 months is:
Continue 2,6,12,20,30 under successive even differences.
questions.explanation: Differences 4,6,8,10; next 12 gives 42.

questions.stem: Under the rule n↦n²+1, 4:17 :: 7:?
Which is not a prime number?
questions.explanation: 21=3×7; the other three have no divisor other than 1 and themselves.

questions.stem: Complete the tool-to-measured-quantity relation: thermometer:temperature :: barometer:?
questions.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

questions.stem: With each letter shifted forward 1, how is CAT encoded?
questions.explanation: C→D,A→B,T→U.

questions.stem: Using A=1,…,Z=26, find the sum of the letter positions in DOG.
If + means multiplication and × means addition, evaluate 4+3×2 using normal precedence after replacement.
questions.explanation: Rewrite 4×3+2=14.

questions.stem: If a code reverses the letters before shifting each forward 1, encode ABZ.
questions.explanation: ABZ reverses to ZBA, then shifts to ACB.

questions.stem: A person walks 3 km east then 4 km north. What is the shortest distance from start?
Facing west, a person turns right. Which way do they face?
questions.explanation: A right turn from west points north.

questions.stem: Walk 5 m north,2 m east,5 m south. The final position is:
questions.explanation: North and south cancel;2 m east remains.

questions.stem: A full turn followed by a half-turn from south leaves the person facing:
questions.explanation: The full turn changes nothing; half-turn reverses south to north.

questions.stem: A person is 6th from the left and 9th from the right. How many people are there?
M is the brother of N. N is the mother of P. What is M to P?
questions.explanation: Mother’s brother is maternal uncle.

questions.stem: If A>B, B=C and C>D, what necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: A>B=C>D implies A>D.

questions.stem: In a line of 21, R is 9th from the left. What is R’s position from the right?
In a group of 60,35 like tea,30 coffee and 15 both. How many like neither?
questions.explanation: Union=35+30−15=50; neither 10.

questions.stem: All roses are flowers. Some roses are red. Which must follow?
questions.explanation: The supplied red roses belong to the flower set.

questions.stem: No poets are pilots. All teachers are poets. Which must follow?
questions.explanation: The teacher subset of poets is disjoint from pilots.

questions.stem: All A are B, with no existence asserted. Which is necessarily valid?
questions.explanation: A⊆B means A has no member outside B; existence is not established.

questions.stem: Talks X,Y,Z run Monday toWednesday. X before Y; Z notWednesday. Which is fixed?
questions.explanation: Valid schedules XZY and ZXY both put Y on Wednesday.

questions.stem: Four seats 1–4 from the reader’s left: B immediately right of A; C in 1; D in 4. Who is in 2?
questions.explanation: C occupies 1,D 4; AB must occupy 2–3.

questions.stem: If A is somewhere left of B in three seats with C otherwise unrestricted, which is possible?
questions.explanation: Only ACB has A left of B.

questions.stem: Five consecutive numbered slots contain a two-slot block AB with A immediately before B. How many starting slots can AB have before other constraints?
questions.explanation: The block can start in 1,2,3 or 4.

questions.stem: An upward arrow is reflected in a horizontal mirror. It points:
questions.explanation: Horizontal reflection reverses the vertical direction.

questions.stem: A right-pointing arrow rotates 90° counterclockwise. It points:
questions.explanation: Counterclockwise from east gives north.

questions.stem: One hole away from a single fold line is punched through two folded layers. After unfolding, how many distinct holes result?
questions.explanation: Reflection across the fold produces a second distinct hole because the original is away from the fold.

questions.stem: A vertical mirror changes the left-to-right sequence of distinct symbols P,Q,R into:
questions.explanation: Reflection reverses left-to-right order.

questions.stem: Sales rose after a shop changed its sign and reduced prices. Which is established?
options: The sign alone caused the rise
The price reduction had no effect
questions.explanation: Only the reported sequence is established; causes are not isolated.

questions.stem: A colleague makes an upsetting remark. Which response best uses emotional regulation?
options: Pause, clarify the issue and respond respectfully
questions.explanation: Pausing and clarifying enables a proportionate response.

questions.stem: Which string exactly matches AB 10 O 5?
questions.explanation: The required sequence is A,B,numeral 1,numeral 0,letter O,numeral 5.

questions.stem: Some inspected files had errors. Which conclusion follows?
options: At least one inspected file had an error
questions.explanation: Some establishes at least one in the inspected set, not a universal claim.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: Each of these books ___ a cover.
questions.explanation: Each is singular here, so has.

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The list of names are ready.
The list of names have ready.
The list of names were ready.
The list of names is ready.
questions.explanation: The head noun list is singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: The students ___ waiting outside.
questions.explanation: Plural students takes are.

questions.stem: Which is a complete standard sentence?
questions.explanation: It has a subject and finite verb and stands as an independent clause.

questions.stem: Correct the verb: Every participant receive a badge.
questions.explanation: Every participant is singular and takes receives.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
options: When the rain stopped, we left.
When the rain stopped we left.
When, the rain stopped we left.
When the rain, stopped we left.
questions.explanation: The introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma in this formal example.

questions.stem: Choose: He ___ here since 2020 and still works here.
questions.explanation: Present perfect links the continuing situation from 2020 to now.

questions.stem: Choose: By the time we arrived, the film ___.
questions.explanation: Past perfect places the beginning before our past arrival.

questions.stem: Choose: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ indoors.
questions.explanation: A real future conditional uses present in the if-clause and will in the result.

questions.stem: Choose the standard hypothetical form: If I ___ you, I would apologise.
questions.explanation: Formal hypothetical were is appropriate.

questions.stem: Choose: At 8 pm yesterday, I ___ dinner.
questions.explanation: Past continuous describes activity underway at a specified past time.

questions.stem: Choose the correct past form: She ___ to Delhi last week.
questions.explanation: Went is the simple past of go.

questions.stem: Choose: ___ hour passed.
questions.explanation: Hour begins with a vowel sound.

questions.stem: Choose: She bought ___ useful tool.
questions.explanation: Useful begins with a /y/ consonant sound.

questions.stem: Choose: He is interested ___ astronomy.
questions.explanation: The standard construction is interested in.

questions.stem: Choose: The meeting starts ___9 am.
questions.explanation: At introduces this clock time.

questions.stem: Choose: We will meet ___ Monday.
questions.explanation: On is used with named days in this construction.

questions.stem: Choose: Success depends ___ preparation.
questions.explanation: The construction is depend on.

questions.stem: Choose the passive of: They repair the road.
options: The road is repaired by them.
The road has repair by them.
questions.explanation: Simple present passive uses is+past participle.

questions.stem: Choose the passive of: She wrote the letter.
options: The letter was written by her.
The letter has wrote by her.
questions.explanation: Simple past passive uses was written.

questions.stem: Choose: The files ___ being checked now.
questions.explanation: Plural files and present continuous passive take are being checked.

questions.stem: Which basic clause has no direct object for ordinary object-to-subject passive conversion?
questions.explanation: Slept is intransitive in this sentence.

questions.stem: Passive of: They will announce the result.
questions.explanation: Keep will and add be+announced.

questions.stem: Passive of: Someone has stolen my bag.
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive is has been+past participle.

questions.stem: In a later past context, report: He said,"I am ready."
options: He said that I am ready.
He said that he was ready.
He told that was he ready.
questions.explanation: Pronoun changes to he and am backshifts to was in the supplied context.

questions.stem: Report a yes–no question: She asked,"Are you ready?"
options: She asked that are you ready.
